summary: Defines IPv6 routing requirements for building automation in low-power and lossy networks. It comes from the ROLL working group, which targets routing in industrial, commercial, home and urban settings. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists what IPv6 routing needs to support in building automation networks. It accounts for thousands of small sensors and controllers, intermittent wireless links and devices that sleep to save power.

questions: how many nodes must a building automation routing protocol support
subtitle: IPv6 routing requirements for building sensors, controllers and actuators

tldr.problem: Building automation networks contain many constrained devices, use lossy links and are often installed before the building's ordinary IP network is ready.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes building systems and traffic, then lists routing requirements for commissioning, scale, mobility, sleeping devices, route selection, management and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document for routing in building low-power and lossy networks; it does not define a routing protocol.

facts.label: Battery-life example
facts.value: At least 5 years with a 2,000 mAh battery

today: RFC 5867 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines building-automation routing requirements and does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: Building Automation Networks
sections.content:
Building management systems connect sensors, actuators, controllers and user interfaces across systems such as heating and ventilation, lighting, security, fire detection and elevators. The RFC defines IPv6 routing requirements for the low-power and lossy networks used in building automation.

Devices may be wired or wireless, and sensors may be battery-powered, battery-less or mains-powered. Actuators and area controllers are mains-powered. The document's system overview provides context; the routing requirements are stated in its requirements section.
sections.plainLanguage: Building systems connect devices that measure conditions and devices that change them. Their routing must work across a mix of wired and wireless equipment with different power limits.

sections.title: Installation and System Structure
sections.content:
A building management system is organized into subsystems, with sensors and actuators at the edges, area controllers for locations such as rooms, and zone controllers for larger logical or physical areas. Nodes may have partial or complete standalone operation if higher system layers are unavailable.

Building systems are commonly installed from endpoints inward: devices are installed and tested in rooms, rooms are joined into subsystems, and the system may later connect to an enterprise network. The RFC notes that building systems may need to operate before services such as DHCP, authentication and DNS are available.
sections.plainLanguage: Installers add and test devices in rooms before joining those rooms into larger systems. The building controls therefore need to work before the office network is ready.

sections.title: Traffic and Recovery Patterns
sections.content:
Most real-time sensor and actuator traffic stays within a local low-power and lossy network (LLN); alarms and event information may travel upward. Sensors send readings to controllers and expect application acknowledgments. Multicast may support commissioning and coordinated actions such as switching a group of lights.

Event-based systems can be quiet during normal operation but produce heavier traffic during startup and firmware updates. After a power disruption, many devices may reconnect while the network has incomplete neighbor information. The RFC therefore calls for adaptive routing that can improve routes as the network stabilizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic is often light during normal operation but can rise when devices start or update. Routing must adapt as devices reconnect and the network learns which paths are usable.

sections.title: Commissioning, Scale and Route Selection
sections.content:
Devices must be able to join without a separate commissioning tool, and local devices should be able to communicate without extra routing infrastructure. A replacement device must be able to advertise both its own IPv6 address and the failed device's old address. The routing protocol must support at least 2,000 nodes, including 1,000 routers and 1,000 hosts, and end-to-end communication between arbitrary devices in the administrative domain.

The RFC sets mobility targets for devices that stop moving: within the same LLN, communication should resume within 5 seconds and the network should converge in under 10 seconds; across LLNs, the respective targets are 10 seconds and under 20 seconds. Routing must support unicast, multicast and anycast, adapt to a route-quality metric, support alternate routes, and prioritize critical traffic. Reactive route discovery should add no more than 120 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must join devices without complex setup and support thousands of nodes. It must also recover communication after movement, choose routes using link quality and give important traffic priority.

sections.title: Constrained Devices and Security
sections.content:
Routing must account for devices with limited memory, processing power and battery energy. Non-routing devices should fit within 128 KB of memory and routing devices within 256 KB of flash, as described in the RFC. The last-hop router must buffer messages for sleeping devices for at least 20 seconds.

Security settings must be configurable and may be raised from installation to commissioning. The routing solutions must support encryption, and authentication should be configurable and occur when a device joins or rejoins rather than at every hop. Security updates must reach sleeping devices when they wake. The RFC says its requirements document introduces no new security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing must fit the memory and battery limits of small devices and save messages for devices that are asleep. The security level can change during installation, but the protocol must support encryption and deliver key updates.
